why: The redaction rules both SDKs apply before anything reaches Temporal history, plus the one the orchestrator applies before anything reaches a stored report. A whole-key match for an ask's fields; two word-in-a-sentence matches for a narration — a secret-shaped assignment, and a bearer/basic credential; and an HTTP-message rule for a report's code blocks. The kinds must NOT be merged with each other — they are different jobs and every implementation argues so in its header — but the LANGUAGES must agree exactly.
why_it_matters: This is the one parity surface where being wrong is a credential written into workflow history, or into a report somebody forwards, in the clear rather than a formatting difference. The implementations were byte-identical when this corpus was written; the risk is a word added to one side and not the other, which narrate.py's own header already named: 'a word only one of them knows is redacted in one surface and not in the other'. The http_headers section arrived with a third language and a third writer, and with two measured leaks in the rules that were already here: a multi-valued `Cookie` was half-redacted, which reads as safe, and a JSON body was not redacted at all.

http_headers.why: the header spec §5 names first, and the commonest credential line there is
the proxy variant, matched by the affix class rather than by being named twice

A MULTI-VALUED COOKIE, WHICH THE SENTENCE RULE HALF-REDACTS. Measured before this rule existed: `Cookie: a=1; b=2` became `Cookie: [redacted] b=2` in BOTH languages — the line reads as safe and the second pair is in the clear. This case is the reason the rule exists.
the response direction, where the leak also took the attributes with it
a header named in §5 and matched through the hyphen affix: api[_-]?key covers Api-Key
the 12-character floor does NOT apply when a header name is present, so a one-character token is still redacted
a header nobody listed, caught because its name ends in a word from the list
a lowercase name with no space after the colon: RFC 9112 permits none
an ordinary header is untouched, which is what keeps a report readable
a status line has no colon-separated name and survives whole
a request line is not a header, so the credential in its query string is caught by the SENTENCE rule instead — this is what §5 means by reusing the existing rules
an empty header value is left alone rather than being marked redacted, because there was nothing there

A NON-BREAKING SPACE AFTER THE COLON. The whitespace classes here are spelled [ \t] and not \s precisely so that all three languages agree on this byte: Go's \s is ASCII-only while Python's and JavaScript's include U+00A0, and this rule runs over a latin-1 view of raw bytes where byte 0xA0 IS U+00A0. The existing sentence rule diverges on it (Go `token:[redacted]`, Python `token:\xa0[redacted]`) and nothing catches that; the new rule does not inherit the problem.

A JSON BODY, WHICH THE SENTENCE RULE MISSES ENTIRELY. Measured: `{"password": "hunter2"}` came back untouched, because the closing quote sits between the key and the colon so \s*[:=]\s* never matches. An http block holding a login request stored the password in the clear.
the same with no spaces and a following member, which must survive
a value containing an escaped quote is redacted whole, and the JSON stays valid — the first implementation ate the closing quote and produced `"[redacted]}`
a key that names nothing secret is untouched, so a report keeps its findings
a whole request: the request line survives, the credential header goes, the content type stays, and the body's password goes — with every CRLF exactly where it was
http_headers.input:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: t.test
Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz
Content-Type: application/json

{"password": "hunter2"}
http_headers.expect:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: t.test
Authorization: [redacted]
Content-Type: application/json

{"password": "[redacted]"}
